yahweh.title: Yahweh
yahweh.summary: The personal name of Israel's God, printed as LORD in most English Bibles.
yahweh.plain: **Nobody calls their own mother "the woman".** Israel's God has an actual name, four Hebrew letters, and almost every English Bible swaps it for the word LORD in small capitals. That substitution is a Jewish habit of reverence that Christian translators inherited. It tells you nothing about what the name means.

el.title: El
el.summary: The ordinary word for god in the region, and also the name of the chief god of Israel's neighbors.
el.plain: **Baker is a job, and it is also somebody's surname.** El works that way across the ancient Near East: the ordinary word for a god, and the personal name of the god at the top of Canaan's pantheon. Israel used it of Yahweh anyway, without apology or explanation.

el-elyon.title: El Elyon
el-elyon.summary: A title meaning Most High, used in the verse where the nations get handed out to different gods.
el-elyon.plain: A title, not a name. It means Most High. **Picture a landlord carving a building into floors and putting a different caretaker over each one.** That is what Deuteronomy 32:8 describes happening to the nations, and who the caretakers are depends on which ancient copy of the verse you read.

el-shaddai.title: El Shaddai
el-shaddai.summary: An old title for Israel's God, translated Almighty, whose actual meaning is disputed.
el-shaddai.plain: **Almighty is a guess that stuck.** The Hebrew behind it, Shadday, has two serious explanations competing: a word for mountain, and a word for the wild country past the edge of the farmland. Greek translators chose a word meaning all-powerful, and English has followed them ever since.

yahweh-tzevaot.title: Yahweh Tzevaot
yahweh-tzevaot.summary: A battle title: the God of armies, meaning heavenly ones rather than Israel's soldiers.
yahweh-tzevaot.plain: **Call a man commander of the forces and nobody pictures him holding a rifle.** This title, God of armies, works the same way. The armies are not Israel's infantry, they are the heavenly host, and the phrase turns up most often in scenes set around a throne.

the-angel-of-yahweh.title: The Angel of Yahweh
the-angel-of-yahweh.summary: A messenger who shows up speaking as God himself, and gets treated as God by the people who meet him.
the-angel-of-yahweh.plain: **A courier who reads a letter aloud is not the person who wrote it.** This figure does not behave like a courier. He speaks as God in the first person, accepts worship, gets called God by the narrator, and is still described as sent by God. The text leaves that tension sitting where it is.

the-commander-of-yahwehs-army.title: The Commander of Yahweh's Army
the-commander-of-yahwehs-army.summary: An armed figure who meets Joshua outside Jericho and refuses to take a side.
the-commander-of-yahwehs-army.plain: Joshua meets an armed man outside Jericho and asks the obvious question: are you for us or for them. **The answer is no.** He has not come to take a side. Joshua pulls his sandals off and worships him, and nobody in the scene corrects him.

the-son-of-man.title: The Son of Man
the-son-of-man.summary: A human-looking figure in Daniel's vision who arrives on the clouds and is handed authority over everything.
the-son-of-man.plain: **Son of man is an ordinary way of saying a human being**, the way we might say a soul. In Daniel 7 someone answering that description arrives riding the clouds, which everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible only God does, and is handed authority over everything. Jesus claims the title at his trial, and that is the moment he is charged with blasphemy.

bene-elohim.title: Bene elohim
bene-elohim.summary: Sons of God: a group of lesser divine beings who show up at God's throne.
bene-elohim.plain: Sons of God. **The phrase works like sons of Israel, which never meant boys with a father called Israel.** It is an idiom for a category, and the category is divine beings. They are plural, created, under God, and standing at his throne.

the-elohim-of-psalm-82.title: The elohim of Psalm 82
the-elohim-of-psalm-82.summary: A psalm where God stands up in a room full of gods and sentences them to death.
the-elohim-of-psalm-82.plain: **A judge can stand up in his own courtroom and sentence the other judges.** That is the scene. God stands in an assembly of gods and passes sentence on them for running the world badly. One Hebrew word, elohim, covers both the one standing and the ones being sentenced.

the-host-of-heaven.title: The host of heaven
the-host-of-heaven.summary: Two things at once: God's heavenly army, and the sun, moon and stars Israel was told not to worship.
the-host-of-heaven.plain: **Host used to mean an army, which is why we still say a host of enemies.** In the Hebrew Bible it does two jobs at once: the army standing around God's throne, and the sun, moon and stars Israel is repeatedly forbidden to worship. Deuteronomy 4:19 ties the two together by saying God allotted those lights to the other nations.

seraphim.title: Seraphim
seraphim.summary: Six-winged beings around God's throne in Isaiah's vision, described with a word that elsewhere means burning serpent.
seraphim.plain: **The word means burning ones, and five of its seven appearances are snakes.** The serpents in the wilderness are seraphim. So are the six-winged figures around the throne in Isaiah's vision. What sits behind the image is an Egyptian winged cobra rather than anything with a harp.

cherubim.title: Cherubim
cherubim.summary: Winged composite creatures that guard and carry God's throne, nothing like the babies in later art.
cherubim.plain: Forget the babies on greeting cards. **Cherubim are composite animals, nearer to the winged bulls with human faces that guarded Assyrian palace doors.** They hold the way back into Eden with a flaming sword, and inside the temple they form the seat God is described as sitting on.

ophanim.title: Ophanim
ophanim.summary: The wheels full of eyes in Ezekiel's vision, which later tradition turned into a class of angel.
ophanim.plain: Wheels, full of eyes, moving alongside the creatures and sharing their spirit. **Ezekiel never says whether they are beings or the machinery of the throne.** Later Jewish tradition made the call for him and filed them as a rank of angel.

the-watchers-of-daniel-4.title: The Watchers of Daniel 4
the-watchers-of-daniel-4.summary: Heavenly figures in one chapter of Daniel who announce a king's downfall.
the-watchers-of-daniel-4.plain: **A watcher is someone who does not sleep**, and the Aramaic word probably comes from the verb to be awake. Three times in a single chapter of Daniel, figures carrying that title come down and announce a king's downfall. Nothing here suggests they have done anything wrong. The fallen Watchers everybody pictures come from 1 Enoch instead.

the-morning-stars.title: The morning stars
the-morning-stars.summary: Stars that sing at the creation of the world, set in parallel with the sons of God.
the-morning-stars.plain: **Hebrew poetry says a thing twice, the second time in different words.** Job pairs the morning stars singing with all the sons of God shouting, which puts the two in one category rather than putting one of them in the sky. They are cheering while the earth is being founded, so they were already there.

michael.title: Michael
michael.summary: The angel assigned to Israel, and the only figure the Bible calls an archangel.
michael.plain: Every nation in Daniel has a spirit figure set over it, and Michael is Israel's. **He is also the only being in the Bible ever called an archangel.** Most of what people picture at the name was filled in by later Jewish writing, which made far more of him than the handful of passages that actually name him.

gabriel.title: Gabriel
gabriel.summary: The angel who explains visions and announces births, named four times in the Bible.
gabriel.plain: Named four times in the whole Bible, twice to Daniel and twice in Luke's opening chapter. **His work is explaining and announcing**, not fighting. Scripture never calls him an archangel, though nearly everyone assumes it does.

the-princes-of-persia-and-greece.title: The princes of Persia and Greece
the-princes-of-persia-and-greece.summary: Spirit figures in Daniel who rule nations and can hold up a messenger from God for weeks.
the-princes-of-persia-and-greece.plain: A messenger is sent to Daniel and turns up three weeks late. **He was held up, and the thing holding him up was the prince of Persia**, with the prince of Greece already waiting behind it. In this chapter nations have beings set over them, and those beings push back.

the-satan-of-job.title: The satan of Job
the-satan-of-job.summary: The accuser in Job, a job title in God's court rather than a personal name.
the-satan-of-job.plain: **Ask for the duty manager and you are asking for whoever is on shift, not for a man called Duty.** The Hebrew in Job puts the word the in front: the accuser. It is a post in God's court. He reports in, asks permission before he acts, and stays inside the limits he is given.

the-lying-spirit.title: The lying spirit
the-lying-spirit.summary: A spirit who volunteers at God's throne to deceive a king's prophets.
the-lying-spirit.plain: A prophet describes God asking a room for volunteers. One spirit steps forward with a plan to fool a king's prophets into promising him a victory he will not get. **God approves the plan and sends it out.** The whole scene is told as the reason the king is about to die.

the-destroyer.title: The destroyer
the-destroyer.summary: The killing figure of the Passover night, later seen again with a drawn sword over Jerusalem.
the-destroyer.plain: On the Passover night something moves through Egypt killing, and blood on the doorframe is what stops it at the door. **The same figure appears again standing over Jerusalem with a drawn sword.** Paul mentions it centuries later without explaining it, as though his readers already knew.

angels.title: Angels
angels.summary: A word that means messenger and describes a job, not a species of being.
angels.plain: **Angel is a job description, like courier.** The Hebrew and Greek words behind it both mean messenger, and both get used of ordinary human messengers too. The word tells you nothing about what kind of being is doing the carrying, which is why using it for everything flattens a very mixed cast into one category.

archangel.title: Archangel
archangel.summary: A rank that appears twice in the New Testament and belongs to Michael alone.
archangel.plain: The word turns up twice in the entire New Testament, and Michael is the only one who ever gets it. **The famous nine ranks of angels are not in the Bible.** They come from a Christian writer of the fifth or sixth century.

the-holy-ones.title: The holy ones
the-holy-ones.summary: A name for the beings who make up God's court.
the-holy-ones.plain: Holy does not mean well behaved here. It means set apart for a god. **The holy ones are the beings who make up God's court**, and Psalm 89 sets the phrase in parallel with another one for divine beings, which is how you can tell it is not talking about Israel.

raphael.title: Raphael
raphael.summary: An angel who works as a physician and demon-binder in Tobit, a book outside the Protestant Bible.
raphael.plain: A traveling companion who turns out to be an angel, cures blindness with fish gall, and ties up a demon. **He is in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and not in the Protestant one**, because the book he appears in sits on the far side of that line.

uriel-sariel-phanuel.title: Uriel, Sariel, Phanuel
uriel-sariel-phanuel.summary: Angels named in 1 Enoch that readers go looking for in the Bible and never find.
uriel-sariel-phanuel.plain: People go hunting for these names in the Bible and never find them. **They come from 1 Enoch**, which lists named archangels with assigned jobs. The names move around between manuscripts, which suggests they work as slots to be filled rather than as fixed individuals.

baal.title: Baal
baal.summary: The storm god of Canaan, Israel's most persistent religious rival, and Elijah's opponent on Mount Carmel.
baal.plain: **The contest on Mount Carmel is not an argument about whether Baal exists.** It is a contest over which god answers by fire, held on a mountain, in the weather, on Baal's own ground. He was the storm god of Canaan and the rival Israel kept going back to for centuries.

baal-zebub-beelzebul.title: Baal-zebub / Beelzebul
baal-zebub-beelzebul.summary: A Philistine god whose name Israel deliberately misspelled into lord of the flies.
baal-zebub-beelzebul.plain: His actual title meant something like prince, or lord of the exalted house. **The Hebrew writers changed one letter and turned it into lord of the flies.** The Greek New Testament keeps the dignified spelling, so the insult belongs to Kings and not to the Gospels.

baal-peor.title: Baal-peor
baal-peor.summary: The local version of Baal tied to an incident where Israel ate meals offered to the dead.
baal-peor.plain: The local Baal of a place called Peor. **Psalm 106 says Israel ate sacrifices offered to the dead there**, which puts this nearer to a cult of the dead than to ordinary idol worship.

baal-berith.title: Baal-berith
baal-berith.summary: Lord of the covenant, worshipped at Shechem, whose temple funded a coup.
baal-berith.plain: Lord of the covenant, worshipped at Shechem, the same town where Joshua had staged a covenant ceremony to Yahweh. **Abimelech pays for his coup out of this temple's treasury.**

hadad-rimmon.title: Hadad / Rimmon
hadad-rimmon.summary: The Syrian storm god, named when a foreign general asks to be excused for bowing in his temple.
hadad-rimmon.plain: The Syrian storm god, Baal's opposite number further north. **He gets named because a foreign general asks to be excused in advance for bowing in his temple**, since the job requires him to stand beside a king who leans on his arm.

asherah.title: Asherah
asherah.summary: A goddess and also the wooden object that stood for her, one of which sat in the Jerusalem temple.
asherah.plain: Two things under one name: a goddess, and the wooden object that stood for her. **That is why English Bibles wander between Asherah, groves and poles without settling.** A carved image of her stood inside the Jerusalem temple under one king.

ashtoreth-astarte.title: Ashtoreth / Astarte
ashtoreth-astarte.summary: A goddess of war and love whose Hebrew name was deliberately mispronounced to mean shame.
ashtoreth-astarte.plain: **Her name in Hebrew is deliberately mispronounced.** The consonants are hers, the vowels are lifted from the word for shame, so the spelling itself is an insult. She was a goddess of war and love, and Saul's armor was hung up in her temple after he died.

the-queen-of-heaven.title: The Queen of Heaven
the-queen-of-heaven.summary: A goddess whose cakes the women of Judah baked, and who told the prophet life was better when they did.
the-queen-of-heaven.plain: The women of Judah baked cakes for her, and when Jeremiah confronted them **they told him to his face that life had been better when they did it.** Her title carries the same doctored vowels as Ashtoreth's, so even the name on the page is an argument.

anat.title: Anat
anat.summary: A violent warrior goddess, prominent among Israel's neighbors and never once named in the Bible.
anat.plain: A violent warrior goddess, everywhere in the texts of Israel's neighbors, and **never once named as a goddess in the Hebrew Bible.** She survives only inside place names and one personal name. Her absence from the prophets is the strange part, given how large she looms at Ugarit.

chemosh.title: Chemosh
chemosh.summary: The god of Moab, and the one foreign god the Bible admits won a battle.
chemosh.plain: Moab's god, and **the one foreign god the Bible lets win a battle.** A Moabite king sacrifices his own son on the city wall, fury comes against Israel, and Israel withdraws. Jephthah argues territory with the Ammonites on the same terms: you keep what Chemosh gives you, we keep what Yahweh gives us.

molech.title: Molech
molech.summary: The god associated with child sacrifice in a valley outside Jerusalem that gave us the word Gehenna.
molech.plain: Child sacrifice in a valley just outside Jerusalem. **That valley's name, Hinnom, is where the word Gehenna comes from**, so the New Testament word usually translated hell is a real place on a map. Two kings of Judah burned their own sons there.

milcom.title: Milcom
milcom.summary: The god of Ammon, a different god from Molech though English Bibles have blurred them.
milcom.plain: Ammon's god, and **not the same god as Molech**, though English Bibles have blurred the two for centuries. Solomon builds shrines for both inside one passage, which is the plainest sign they are not one god with two spellings.

dagon.title: Dagon
dagon.summary: The god of the Philistines, whose statue falls and breaks in front of Israel's ark.
dagon.plain: The Philistine god whose statue falls on its face in front of Israel's captured ark, twice, losing its head and hands on the threshold the second time. **It reads like slapstick and is not.** It is a legal picture: the beaten vassal face down in front of his overlord.

nisroch.title: Nisroch
nisroch.summary: The god in whose temple an Assyrian king was murdered by his own sons.
nisroch.plain: An Assyrian king is murdered by his own sons while worshipping in this god's temple. **The name appears in no Assyrian source**, which has produced two centuries of proposed corrections and no agreement.

nergal.title: Nergal
nergal.summary: A Mesopotamian god of plague and the underworld, brought into Samaria by resettled foreigners.
nergal.plain: Brought into Samaria by people the Assyrians resettled there. **In Mesopotamia he is the god you blame for plague**, along with drought, famine, fire and sudden death, and kings called on him before going out on campaign.

nebo.title: Nebo
nebo.summary: The Babylonian god of scribes, shown being hauled out of town on pack animals in Isaiah's parody.
nebo.plain: The Babylonian god of scribes, appearing exactly once. **Isaiah shows him loaded onto pack animals and hauled out of town.** The joke works because Babylon really did parade his image through the streets at New Year, and Isaiah turns the parade into a retreat.

bel-marduk.title: Bel / Marduk
bel-marduk.summary: The chief god of Babylon, named in the prophets as a god about to be humiliated.
bel-marduk.plain: Bel is a title meaning lord, and it sticks to Marduk, the chief god of Babylon. **Jeremiah names both in a single line**, a small sign that the prophets knew the foreign pantheon by name rather than waving at it from a distance.

tammuz.title: Tammuz
tammuz.summary: A dying shepherd god whose women mourners Ezekiel sees weeping at the temple gate.
tammuz.plain: Ezekiel is shown women weeping for him at the north gate of the temple, one of four things he is made to look at, each worse than the last. **He is usually introduced as a vegetation god, and that is a later simplification.** In the Sumerian material he starts out as a shepherd.

adrammelech-and-anammelech.title: Adrammelech and Anammelech
adrammelech-and-anammelech.summary: Two gods of resettled foreigners, named in the one verse that says their people burned children to them.
adrammelech-and-anammelech.plain: Two gods of resettled foreigners, named in the single verse that records their people burning children to them. **Both names end in the word for king**, the same element sitting inside Molech's.

ashima-nibhaz-tartak-succoth-benoth.title: Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Succoth-benoth
ashima-nibhaz-tartak-succoth-benoth.summary: Four imported gods named once each and never mentioned again.
ashima-nibhaz-tartak-succoth-benoth.plain: Four gods brought in by settlers after the northern deportations, each named once and never mentioned again. **They are here because they are the dead ends.** A list of divine names that quietly drops the ones with no follow-up is not telling you the truth about the material.

sikkuth-and-kiyyun-rephan.title: Sikkuth and Kiyyun / Rephan
sikkuth-and-kiyyun-rephan.summary: Star gods carried in procession, where the Greek Bible and the Hebrew give different names.
sikkuth-and-kiyyun-rephan.plain: Star gods carried along in procession. **Stephen quotes the Greek Old Testament and says Rephan where the Hebrew says Kiyyun**, which is a short clean case of a New Testament speaker quoting a translation rather than the Hebrew.

gad-and-meni.title: Gad and Meni
gad-and-meni.summary: Fortune and Destiny, two gods most readers never notice are in the verse.
gad-and-meni.plain: Fortune and Destiny, with a table laid for them and wine poured out. **Most readers walk past them because English versions turn the two names back into common nouns.** The Greek translators read both as real gods.

zeus.title: Zeus
zeus.summary: The chief Greek god, whom a crowd mistakes Barnabas for.
zeus.plain: A crowd at Lystra decides Barnabas is Zeus, and the local priest arrives at the gates with oxen and garlands. **It is one of the few places in the New Testament that shows pagan worship happening rather than describing it.**

hermes.title: Hermes
hermes.summary: The Greek messenger god, whom the same crowd mistakes Paul for because he did the talking.
hermes.plain: The same crowd decides Paul is Hermes, **and Luke tells you why: Paul was the one doing the talking.** Hermes was the messenger and the interpreter, so the guess is exact rather than random.

artemis-of-the-ephesians.title: Artemis of the Ephesians
artemis-of-the-ephesians.summary: A local goddess whose souvenir trade started a riot against Paul.
artemis-of-the-ephesians.plain: A riot starts over Paul, and **it starts in the souvenir trade.** The silversmiths making her shrines were losing money. The city clerk calms everyone by appealing to the image that fell from heaven, a stock claim made for a good many statues.

the-dioscuri.title: The Dioscuri
the-dioscuri.summary: Twin gods who protected sailors, carved on the ship that carried Paul to Rome.
the-dioscuri.plain: Castor and Pollux, the twins carved on the bow of the ship that carried Paul to Rome. **Sailors trusted them because of St Elmo's fire**, the glow that sometimes appears on a mast in a storm, read as the twins turning up. Luke records the figurehead and says nothing about it.

the-unknown-god.title: The unknown god
the-unknown-god.summary: An Athenian altar hedging against offending a god nobody could name, which Paul preached from.
the-unknown-god.plain: Athens kept an altar hedging against offending a god nobody had named. **Paul preaches from it.** The practice was real rather than something Luke invented for the scene; travelers were still describing these altars a century later.

the-python-spirit.title: The python spirit
the-python-spirit.summary: A fortune-telling spirit named after the oracle at Delphi, cast out of a slave girl.
the-python-spirit.plain: A slave girl tells fortunes, and the Greek calls the thing inside her a python, the word for the oracle at Delphi. **Luke never says she was a fraud.** He has Paul cast out the thing that was making her right.

mot.title: Mot
mot.summary: Death as a figure with an open throat that is never full.
mot.plain: Death, with a throat open and never full, climbing in through the windows, and a covenant made with him. **The argument is whether that is a figure of speech or the memory of a god the neighbors actually worshipped.**

yam.title: Yam
yam.summary: The sea as an opponent God fights, not just water.
yam.plain: The sea. **God rebukes it, splits it, and tramples its waves**, which is not how anyone talks about water. Hebrew poetry keeps leaving open whether the sea here is scenery or an opponent.

leviathan.title: Leviathan
leviathan.summary: A sea monster God crushes in one poem and plays with in another.
leviathan.plain: A sea monster, and the Bible cannot seem to agree what to do with it. **One psalm has God crushing its heads; another has it splashing about in a sea God made for it to play in.** Isaiah puts its death in the future. The same creature is a defeated enemy, a pet, and a job still outstanding.

behemoth.title: Behemoth
behemoth.summary: A huge land beast in Job that nobody has been able to identify.
behemoth.plain: A huge land animal in Job that nobody has pinned down. Hippo, elephant and mythical bull have all been argued, **and every one of them strains some line of the description.** The Hebrew is a plural form doing singular duty, which does not help.

rahab.title: Rahab
rahab.summary: A chaos monster God cuts to pieces, and also a nickname for Egypt.
rahab.plain: A chaos monster God cuts to pieces, **and also a nickname for Egypt.** The two go together rather than being an accident of spelling: Isaiah uses the monster's defeat to mean the Exodus. Job mentions the helpers of Rahab bowing down, which implies a whole company of them.

tannin.title: Tannin
tannin.summary: Sea monsters, which Genesis pointedly lists among the things God made and called good.
tannin.plain: Sea monsters. **Genesis 1 puts them in the column of things God made and called good**, which is a pointed thing to do with a word that everywhere else means the enemy in the water. A psalm later calls them into the choir.

resheph.title: Resheph
resheph.summary: A plague god reduced in the Bible to a word for disease, who still walks at God's feet in one poem.
resheph.plain: A plague god among Israel's neighbors, flattened in most English Bibles into a common noun: plague, flame, burning coal. **In Habakkuk 3 he walks at God's feet**, and a burning coal does not walk anywhere.

deber-and-qeteb.title: Deber and Qeteb
deber-and-qeteb.summary: Pestilence and Destruction, named in a psalm in a way that sounds like a list of beings.
deber-and-qeteb.plain: Pestilence and Destruction. Psalm 91 lists four threats in a shape that reads more like a roll call of named powers than a list of hazards, **and Habakkuk marches Deber along in front of God like an attendant.** The Ugaritic texts pair the same two as gods.

shahar-and-shalem.title: Shahar and Shalem
shahar-and-shalem.summary: Dawn and Dusk as divine figures, one of whom is the father of the shining one in Isaiah 14.
shahar-and-shalem.plain: Dawn and Dusk, treated as figures rather than times of day. **Isaiah 14 calls its falling star the son of Shahar**, and that phrase only carries weight if Shahar is somebody. The Ugaritic texts make the pair divine twins.

the-watchers-enochic.title: The Watchers (Enochic)
the-watchers-enochic.summary: Angels who, in 1 Enoch, come down to earth, marry women, and teach humanity things it should not know.
the-watchers-enochic.plain: In Daniel the word watcher is neutral. **The version everybody actually means comes from 1 Enoch**, where two hundred of them come down on Mount Hermon under a shared oath, marry women, and teach humanity metalwork, weapons, cosmetics and sorcery. That book is not in the Protestant Bible, and Jude quotes it.

shemihazah.title: Shemihazah
shemihazah.summary: The leader who talks the other Watchers into the descent and binds them to an oath.
shemihazah.plain: The one who proposes the descent and **makes the others swear an oath so nobody can back out later.** He is a leader with a command structure under him, twenty chiefs of ten. He is not in the Bible; he is in 1 Enoch.

asael.title: Asael
asael.summary: The Watcher who teaches weapons and cosmetics and gets buried under rocks until judgment.
asael.plain: The Watcher who teaches metalwork, weapons and cosmetics, which 1 Enoch treats as one corruption rather than three. **He is bound hand and foot and thrown into a hole in the desert to wait for judgment**, an image later readers connect to the goat sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement.

azazel.title: Azazel
azazel.summary: The name on the second lot at the Day of Atonement, where the other lot says God.
azazel.plain: On the Day of Atonement two lots are cast over two goats. **One lot says for Yahweh. The other says for Azazel.** That parallel is what makes it hard to read Azazel as a place name, because the other side of the pair is not a place.

nephilim.title: Nephilim
nephilim.summary: The giants of Genesis 6, born from the sons of God and human women.
nephilim.plain: The giants of Genesis 6, born to the sons of God and human women. **Two verses in the entire Hebrew Bible**, and one of them adds that they were around afterward as well, which is the clause the spies' report in Numbers 13 hangs on.

gibborim.title: Gibborim
gibborim.summary: The mighty men of old, a word used of ordinary warriors too.
gibborim.plain: The mighty men of old, the men of renown. **The same word describes David's soldiers**, so it carries nothing supernatural on its own. Genesis 6 supplies that from the sentence around it, not from the word.

rephaim.title: Rephaim
rephaim.summary: A people of giants in some texts and the shades of the dead in others.
rephaim.plain: One word doing two jobs that seem unrelated: a people of giants in the conquest accounts, and the shades of the dead in the poetry. **Isaiah has the grave stirring up the Rephaim to greet a king arriving there.** The overlap is not a translation accident.

anakim.title: Anakim
anakim.summary: The giant clan at Hebron whose size made the Israelite spies call themselves grasshoppers.
anakim.plain: The giant clan at Hebron. **The Israelite spies come back saying they felt like grasshoppers next to them**, and the survivors are noted as having ended up in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. Gath is where Goliath comes from later.

emim-zamzummim-zuzim.title: Emim, Zamzummim, Zuzim
emim-zamzummim-zuzim.summary: What Moab and Ammon called the same giants everyone else called Rephaim.
emim-zamzummim-zuzim.plain: Three names for one thing. **Moab called them Emim, Ammon called them Zamzummim**, and Deuteronomy counts both as Rephaim, so the passage works as a gazetteer of what different neighbors called the same giants.

og-of-bashan.title: Og of Bashan
og-of-bashan.summary: A giant king whose iron bed was thirteen feet long.
og-of-bashan.plain: A giant king, and the Bible gives you his bed: nine cubits long, about thirteen feet. **He ruled Bashan**, which the Ugaritic texts connect with the dead and with the entrance to the underworld, so the location is doing work as well as the measurements.

goliath-and-the-sons-of-rapha.title: Goliath and the sons of Rapha
goliath-and-the-sons-of-rapha.summary: The giant David killed, and the relatives of his who show up later in the same books.
goliath-and-the-sons-of-rapha.plain: Goliath is the famous one, and **he is not the only one.** Second Samuel lists four more from Gath, killed by four of David's men, including one with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.

satan-ho-satanas.title: Satan (ho satanas)
satan-ho-satanas.summary: The name the New Testament gives the chief adversary, a role that had become a name.
satan-ho-satanas.plain: In the Hebrew Bible the word is a job: the accuser. **By the New Testament it has hardened into a name**, and Revelation 12 works like a glossary entry, tying the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan together as one figure.

the-devil-diabolos.title: The devil (diabolos)
the-devil-diabolos.summary: The Greek word for slanderer, used interchangeably with Satan.
the-devil-diabolos.plain: **Devil is just the Greek word for slanderer.** It is what the Greek Old Testament used to translate the Hebrew word for accuser, so the two terms cover the same ground. Centuries of English usage have loaded the word with freight the Greek never carried.

beelzebul.title: Beelzebul
beelzebul.summary: The name Jesus's opponents used for the ruler of demons when they accused him.
beelzebul.plain: When Jesus's opponents want to explain how he casts out demons, **this is the name they reach for: the ruler of the demons.** His answer is the one about a divided kingdom, and about tying up the strong man before robbing his house.

belial-beliar.title: Belial / Beliar
belial-beliar.summary: A Hebrew word for worthlessness that hardened into a name for the enemy of God.
belial-beliar.plain: In Hebrew it is a noun meaning worthlessness, which is why older Bibles have phrases like sons of Belial. **By the time Paul uses it, it has become a name**, set directly opposite Christ.

daimonion.title: Daimonion
daimonion.summary: The New Testament word for demon, borrowed from a Greek word that was morally neutral.
daimonion.plain: **In ordinary Greek a daimon was neither good nor bad**, a middling being between gods and people. The New Testament only ever uses it for the bad kind. Paul's line is that the idol itself is nothing, and the thing behind it is not nothing.

shedim.title: Shedim
shedim.summary: A Hebrew word for the beings Israel sacrificed to, translated demons in Greek.
shedim.plain: Two appearances, both about sacrificing to them, both calling them gods Israel had not known, new arrivals their fathers never feared. **The Greek translators rendered the word demons**, and that is the hinge connecting the Hebrew category to the New Testament one.

seirim.title: Se'irim
seirim.summary: Goat demons, banned as objects of sacrifice and pictured haunting ruins.
seirim.plain: Goat demons. **Leviticus forbids sacrificing to them, and nobody writes a law like that about livestock.** Isaiah has them in ruined cities calling to each other, which is the other half of the picture.

lilith.title: Lilith
lilith.summary: A night demon named once in Isaiah, in a list of creatures living in a ruin.
lilith.plain: One appearance, in a list of creatures left living in a ruin. **English versions cannot agree whether she is a night creature, a screech owl or a night monster.** Everything else people know about Lilith comes from later Jewish writing, not from this verse.

the-dragon.title: The dragon
the-dragon.summary: The beast of Revelation, identified there as the serpent, the devil and Satan all at once.
the-dragon.plain: Revelation stops and tells you who this is: the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan, all one figure. **The tail that sweeps a third of the stars is describing his following**, not reporting a prehistoric fall that happened before the book opens.

the-ancient-serpent.title: The ancient serpent
the-ancient-serpent.summary: The talking serpent of Eden, which the New Testament identifies with Satan though Genesis never does.
the-ancient-serpent.plain: **Genesis never calls the serpent Satan.** That connection is made in the New Testament and read back. What keeps Genesis 3 from being a story about a talking animal is the Hebrew word itself, which plays across serpent, shining one and diviner at the same time.

the-beast-from-the-sea.title: The beast from the sea
the-beast-from-the-sea.summary: The empire-beast of Revelation carrying the famous number.
the-beast-from-the-sea.plain: Daniel's four beasts folded into one, coming up out of the sea and handed its authority by the dragon. **This is the one carrying the famous number**, which the text introduces by saying it takes wisdom to work out.

the-beast-from-the-earth-the-false-proph.title: The beast from the earth / the false prophet
the-beast-from-the-earth-the-false-proph.summary: The second beast of Revelation, which looks like a lamb and talks like a dragon.
the-beast-from-the-earth-the-false-proph.plain: The second beast. **It has two horns like a lamb and speaks like a dragon**, which is the whole point of it: the thing that looks harmless and sounds like the enemy. Later in the book it is simply called the false prophet.

the-man-of-lawlessness.title: The man of lawlessness
the-man-of-lawlessness.summary: An end-times figure Paul describes and refuses to explain.
the-man-of-lawlessness.plain: Paul describes an end-times figure, says his readers already know what is holding him back, **and never says what that is.** Nobody since has settled it. The word antichrist, which people reach for here, is not Paul's word and is not in this passage.

the-ruler-of-this-world.title: The ruler of this world
the-ruler-of-this-world.summary: John's title for Satan, conceding real authority and announcing its end.
the-ruler-of-this-world.plain: John's title for Satan, used three times and every time around the cross. **It grants him a real jurisdiction and announces the end of it in the same breath.**

the-prince-of-the-power-of-the-air.title: The prince of the power of the air
the-prince-of-the-power-of-the-air.summary: Paul's title for the ruling evil power, with the air meaning contested territory overhead.
the-prince-of-the-power-of-the-air.plain: Paul's title for the ruling hostile power. **The air here is not weather.** Ancient cosmology treated the space overhead as contested ground, occupied territory between earth and the higher heavens, and Paul is naming who holds it.

the-god-of-this-age.title: The god of this age
the-god-of-this-age.summary: Paul calls the blinder of unbelievers a god, and translators have to decide what case to use.
the-god-of-this-age.plain: Paul calls him a god. **Greek has no way to distinguish god from God, so the lowercase g in your Bible is a decision an English translator made**, not something the text does.

archai-exousiai-thronoi-kyriotetes.title: Archai, exousiai, thronoi, kyriotetes
archai-exousiai-thronoi-kyriotetes.summary: Paul's vocabulary for ranks of cosmic powers: rulers, authorities, thrones, dominions.
archai-exousiai-thronoi-kyriotetes.plain: Rulers, authorities, thrones, dominions: Paul's vocabulary for ranks of cosmic powers. **Colossians has Christ creating them in one chapter and disarming them in the next**, which tells you they are real beings that went wrong rather than metaphors for human institutions.

stoicheia.title: Stoicheia
stoicheia.summary: A word meaning basic elements that Paul uses for something people can be enslaved to.
stoicheia.plain: The word means basic elements, the ABCs of something. In Hebrews it plainly means the beginner stuff. **In Galatians it sits in parallel with beings that are not gods by nature**, so the same word is doing two different jobs inside one Bible.

legion.title: Legion
legion.summary: The demon who gives his name as a number, in the story that ends with the pigs.
legion.plain: Asked for his name, the demon answers with a number. **The scene happens across the lake in the Decapolis**, the territory the Enochic tradition ties to the spirits of the dead giants, so the geography is carrying part of the argument. Then come the pigs.

abaddon-apollyon.title: Abaddon / Apollyon
abaddon-apollyon.summary: A word for the place of destruction that Revelation turns into an angel over the abyss.
abaddon-apollyon.plain: In the Old Testament the word names a place, destruction, paired with the grave. **Revelation turns it into somebody**: the angel of the abyss, king of the locusts, and gives the name twice, once in Hebrew and once in Greek.

death-and-hades.title: Death and Hades
death-and-hades.summary: Death and the grave, treated in Revelation as figures who ride and get thrown into fire.
death-and-hades.plain: Death and the grave get handed a horse to ride, and later get thrown into the lake of fire. **That is an odd fate for an abstraction.** Paul calls death the last enemy to be destroyed, which reads the same way.

the-four-angels-of-the-euphrates.title: The four angels of the Euphrates
the-four-angels-of-the-euphrates.summary: Angels tied up at a river and released on schedule to kill.
the-four-angels-of-the-euphrates.plain: Four angels tied up at a river and let loose at an appointed hour to kill a third of mankind. **Bound, then released on a schedule somebody else set**, which is how the Watchers are handled too.

lucifer.title: Lucifer
lucifer.summary: Not a name and not Satan: a Latin word for the morning star, used of a Babylonian king.
lucifer.plain: **Lucifer is not a name and never was.** It is an ordinary Latin word for the morning star, used by the Vulgate to translate a Hebrew phrase meaning shining one, son of Dawn. The passage is addressed to a Babylonian king. Capitalizing the Latin common noun into somebody's name is where the whole thing starts.

satan-the-worship-leader.title: Satan the worship leader
satan-the-worship-leader.summary: The belief that Satan ran music in heaven, built on one obscure verse about stone settings.
satan-the-worship-leader.plain: The belief that Satan ran the music in heaven **rests on one obscure verse about settings for stones**, which the King James rendered with tabrets and pipes. Even reading those as instruments, an instrument is not a job title.

mammon.title: Mammon
mammon.summary: An Aramaic word for money that Jesus personified, later mistaken for a demon.
mammon.plain: An Aramaic word for money. **Jesus personifies it as a rival master you cannot serve alongside God**, which is a way of talking, not a demon. Nobody in the ancient world worshipped a god called Mammon.

jehovah.title: Jehovah
jehovah.summary: Not a name anyone in the Bible used, but a misreading of God's name produced centuries later.
jehovah.plain: **Nobody in the Bible ever said this name.** It is God's four Hebrew consonants read with the vowels of a completely different word, a reminder to say Lord instead. Sixteenth-century Christian scholars mistook the reading aid for the word itself.

the-third-of-the-angels.title: The third of the angels
the-third-of-the-angels.summary: The claim that a third of the angels fell with Satan, which no passage actually reports.
the-third-of-the-angels.plain: **No passage in Scripture reports a prehistoric angelic rebellion, and none gives a headcount.** The one third comes from a dragon's tail sweeping stars in a vision of the end, and the arithmetic gets carried backward to an event the Bible never narrates.

lilith-adams-first-wife.title: Lilith, Adam's first wife
lilith-adams-first-wife.summary: A medieval story, not a biblical one.
lilith-adams-first-wife.plain: **The story is medieval, not biblical.** It comes from the Alphabet of Ben Sira, written in Iraq somewhere around the ninth or tenth century. The argument now attached to it, about two different creation accounts, is more recent still.

the-nephilim-as-extraterrestrials.title: The Nephilim as extraterrestrials
the-nephilim-as-extraterrestrials.summary: The claim that the giants of Genesis were aliens, which rests on mistranslated Sumerian.
the-nephilim-as-extraterrestrials.plain: **Assyriologists reject this reading of the Sumerian texts on language grounds, not religious ones.** The words do not say what the claim needs them to say. The biblical material says less than the fringe version and more than the tidied-up version, and both halves of that are worth keeping.

the-ghost-of-samuel.title: The ghost of Samuel
the-ghost-of-samuel.summary: The dead prophet called up by a medium, in a scene that terrifies the medium herself.
the-ghost-of-samuel.plain: A medium calls up the dead prophet, **and the thing that frightens her is what actually comes up.** The narrator calls him Samuel, and the message he gives turns out to be accurate. The idea that a demon was impersonating him is a later attempt to tidy the scene.

dagon-the-fish-god.title: Dagon the fish god
dagon-the-fish-god.summary: The belief that the Philistine god was part fish, which comes from medieval wordplay.
dagon-the-fish-god.plain: **The fish tail comes from a medieval pun, not from anything ancient.** A Hebrew word that sounds like the god's name means fish, a commentator ran with it, and the mermaid pictures followed. What the name actually means is still unresolved.

easter-from-ishtar.title: Easter from Ishtar
easter-from-ishtar.summary: The claim that Easter is named after a Babylonian goddess, which fails as word history.
easter-from-ishtar.plain: **This is a claim about word history, and word history is where it fails.** The English name comes from an old spring month. Almost every other language calls the feast some form of Pascha, which is Passover. The Ishtar chain traces back to one nineteenth-century book.
